description: The number 2272 does not appear directly in the biblical texts and has no well-established symbolic meaning in Jewish numerology or gematria tradition. The closest biblical number is 2172, which in Ezra 2:3 indicates the number of descendants of Parosh who returned to Judah after the Babylonian exile under Zerubbabel's leadership. The census list in Ezra chapter 2 serves as an important historical and theological marker of God's faithfulness in restoring His people to the promised land. The clan of Parosh was among the largest groups that returned, testifying to this family's prominent role in the post-exilic community.

versions.description: The number 2272 appears in Ezra 2:3, where it indicates the number of descendants of Parosh who returned to Judah after the Babylonian exile. This census is part of the great list of returning exiled Jews under Zerubbabel's leadership, as documented in Ezra chapter 2. The list serves as an important historical and theological marker of God's faithfulness in restoring His people to the promised land. The Parosh clan was one of the largest groups that returned, suggesting this was a prominent family in the post-exilic community. Beyond this specific census context, the number 2272 has no well-established symbolic meaning in Jewish numerology or gematria tradition.

footnotes.text: The family of Parosh is also mentioned in Nehemiah 7:8, but there the number given is 2172. Such variations in numbers between the lists in Ezra and Nehemiah are well known and have been the subject of much discussion among biblical scholars. The differences may be due to different times of recording or copyist errors in the transmission of the text.
The name Parosh (פַּרְעֹשׁ) means 'flea' in Hebrew. Despite the humble name, this was a significant clan also mentioned among those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 10:15.

The census list in Ezra 2 has a parallel in Nehemiah 7 and in the apocryphal book 1 Esdras 5. These lists were kept as official documents and served as proof of lineage, which was crucial for claiming property rights and participating in temple worship after the return.
